requirements.product_understanding: A collaborative document editor that allows multiple users to simultaneously edit the same document and see each other's changes in real-time. The system must handle network interruptions gracefully by queuing edits during brief disconnections and reconciling changes when users reconnect, ensuring all users eventually see the same final document version regardless of editing order or timing.
users_and_use_cases: Team members who simultaneously edit documents and need to see each other's changes live
Users who experience brief network drops during editing sessions
Multiple concurrent editors working on the same document at the same time
functional: Support up to 50 simultaneous editors per document
Enable real-time collaborative editing with live updates
Queue edits during brief network disconnections
Reconcile and apply queued edits upon network reconnection
Ensure all users see identical final document versions regardless of edit order or timing
non_functional: Support 500,000 documents with active concurrent editors
Prevent data loss during brief network interruptions
assumptions: Network drops are brief enough to queue edits without user intervention
Users will not experience extended outages that exceed the system's ability to maintain edit queues
The 50 editors per document limit is a hard constraint that won't be exceeded
Document editing sessions will have reasonable duration and frequency patterns
The $40,000 monthly budget covers all infrastructure and operational costs for the specified scale
open_questions: What constitutes a 'brief network drop' in terms of time duration?
How should the system handle conflicts when multiple users edit the same section simultaneously?
What is the expected average document size and complexity to inform storage and processing requirements?
Should there be any limits on how long edit queues can be maintained before forcing reconciliation?
What level of consistency is required - eventual consistency or strong consistency for all operations?

components.name: Document Engine
components.description: Core component responsible for managing document state, applying edits, and handling conflict resolution using Operational Transformation (OT) or Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDT). Processes real-time edits from users and maintains a consistent document view across all clients. Handles the convergence of edits from multiple concurrent editors into a single final document state regardless of order or timing. Scales horizontally to support 500,000 documents with up to 50 concurrent editors per document, operating within the $40,000 monthly budget constraint. Maintains 99.9% availability target through replication and failover mechanisms. Uses a hybrid approach of OT for simple edits and CRDT for complex structural changes to optimize performance while ensuring consistency. Stores document state in memory with periodic snapshots to disk for recovery purposes. Processes up to 10,000 concurrent edit operations per second across all documents, with each operation taking less than 5ms on average. Implements a sharded architecture where documents are distributed across multiple instances based on consistent hashing to enable true horizontal scaling. The component is the only one that can modify document state directly, ensuring consistency through atomic operations. Uses a persistent connection model for real-time updates and handles network disconnections by queuing edits in a centralized service before reconciliation upon reconnection. Maintains a 10-second timeout for edit queues to prevent indefinite buffering of stale changes. Processes edit history in batches of 100 operations to optimize memory usage and reduce latency during conflict resolution. Implements a two-phase commit protocol for critical document modifications to ensure atomicity across distributed systems. This component is the only one that can modify document state directly, ensuring consistency through atomic operations. Decomposed into separate services for document state management, conflict resolution algorithms, and atomic write operations to improve scalability and maintainability.

components.name: Connection Manager
components.description: Manages real-time WebSocket connections between clients and Document Engine components. Handles connection lifecycle events including establishment, disconnection, and reconnection. Forwards edits to the centralized Edit Queue Service upon reconnection instead of queuing locally. Implements a backpressure mechanism to prevent overwhelming the system during high-traffic periods. Maintains connection state for up to 50 concurrent editors per document with automatic cleanup of inactive connections after 30 minutes of inactivity. Uses a connection pooling strategy to optimize resource utilization and reduce latency during connection establishment. Tracks user presence and session information for each document. Implements a heartbeat mechanism to detect and handle dead connections proactively. Handles client-side reconnection logic including resynchronization of local edit queue with server state. Processes up to 20,000 concurrent WebSocket connections across all documents while maintaining <10ms latency for connection establishment. Operates within the $40,000 monthly budget constraint and maintains 99.9% availability target through redundant connection handling. Uses a distributed architecture with multiple instances to ensure no single point of failure. Implements automatic load balancing between Document Engine instances based on current connection count and resource utilization. Implements retry mechanism with exponential backoff when forwarding edits to Edit Queue Service, and adds local buffering capability on the client-side to temporarily store edits if the queue service is unreachable.

components.name: Edit Queue Service
components.description: Dedicated service for storing and managing edit queues during network disconnections. Maintains a queue per user per document with automatic cleanup of completed or expired queues. Stores queued edits in persistent storage (Redis with persistence) to prevent data loss during system failures. Implements a priority-based queuing system where newer edits take precedence over older ones to minimize staleness. Uses a time-based expiration mechanism to prevent indefinite buffering of edits, with a default timeout of 10 seconds before forcing reconciliation. Processes up to 100,000 queued edit operations across all documents while maintaining <5ms latency for queue operations. Handles concurrent access to queues using atomic operations to ensure data integrity during simultaneous read/write operations. Implements a sliding window algorithm to limit queue size and prevent memory exhaustion. The service is optimized for high-throughput scenarios with minimal latency impact on real-time editing performance. Operates within the $40,000 monthly budget constraint and maintains 99.9% availability target through replication and failover mechanisms. Uses a distributed architecture with multiple instances to ensure no single point of failure. Implements automatic scaling based on queue depth and system load to optimize resource utilization. Adds cryptographic signatures (e.g., HMAC-SHA256) to all messages forwarded from Connection Manager to Edit Queue Service, ensuring that the edit queue contents cannot be modified in transit and that only legitimate connection managers can submit edits for queuing.

components.name: Document Storage
components.description: Persistent storage layer for document snapshots, edit history, and metadata. Uses a combination of in-memory cache for active documents and durable storage for archived content. Implements a write-through caching strategy with automatic flushing to persistent storage every 5 seconds for active documents. Maintains document version history with support for rollback operations and audit trails. Handles large document sizes up to 10MB per document with optimized storage formats for efficient retrieval and processing. Uses a distributed storage system with replication across multiple availability zones to ensure high availability and durability. Implements automatic backup and recovery procedures with point-in-time restore capabilities. Processes up to 50,000 document read/write operations per second while maintaining <10ms latency for critical operations. Operates within the $40,000 monthly budget constraint and maintains 99.9% availability target through replication and failover mechanisms. Uses a hybrid storage approach combining SSDs for active documents with cheaper storage for archived content. Implements automatic compaction of edit history to reduce storage overhead while maintaining version integrity. The component ensures no data loss during brief network interruptions by persisting document state regularly and providing recovery mechanisms for disconnected sessions. Implements write-ahead logging (WAL) or similar transactional persistence mechanism on top of the 5-second flush interval to ensure that all edit operations are durably recorded before being acknowledged to clients, meeting RPO requirements for brief interruptions.

architecture.infrastructure: The system uses a distributed architecture with multiple components deployed across cloud infrastructure. The Document Engine and Connection Manager are horizontally scalable services that can be scaled independently based on load requirements. The Edit Queue Service operates as a dedicated microservice with optimized persistent storage for high-throughput scenarios. Document Storage utilizes a hybrid storage approach combining in-memory caching with durable persistent storage for active documents. All components are deployed with redundancy across multiple availability zones to ensure 99.9% availability target. Network traffic is load balanced using a combination of DNS-based routing and application-level load balancing. The system uses containerization with orchestration via Kubernetes for deployment management and scaling automation. Infrastructure monitoring and alerting systems are implemented to track performance metrics and ensure service level agreements are maintained within the $40,000 monthly budget constraint. Redis cluster with multi-master replication across availability zones is implemented to prevent data loss during Redis instance failures, ensuring 99.9% availability target compliance for Edit Queue Service.

decisions.decision: Use of Operational Transformation with CRDT fallback
decisions.alternatives_considered: Operational Transformation (OT) for real-time collaboration, Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDT), and traditional version control approaches
decisions.trade_offs: OT provides strong consistency but is complex to implement correctly; CRDT offers simpler implementation but may have performance overhead; traditional version control would require complex merge logic
decisions.rationale: This approach was chosen because it provides the best balance of consistency guarantees and performance for collaborative editing. OT ensures strong consistency for simple text operations while CRDT handles complex structural changes where OT might be insufficient. The hybrid approach allows for optimal performance while maintaining data integrity under all conditions, meeting the requirement to prevent data loss during brief network interruptions. A unified conflict resolution pipeline was implemented to handle transitions between OT and CRDT operations consistently.

decisions.alternatives_considered: Multi-writer with optimistic locking, single-writer with sharding, and distributed consensus protocols like Raft or Paxos
decisions.trade_offs: Single-writer provides strong consistency but limits parallelism; multi-writer offers better throughput but introduces complexity in conflict resolution; distributed consensus protocols provide strong guarantees but require significant overhead
decisions.rationale: This decision was made to ensure data consistency and prevent race conditions during edit application while maintaining reasonable performance. The sharded architecture with consistent hashing allows for true horizontal scaling across multiple Document Engine instances, eliminating the single-writer bottleneck that would otherwise create a severe scalability constraint. This design choice directly addresses the requirement that all users see identical final document versions regardless of edit order or timing, while keeping complexity manageable within the budget constraints.

decisions.decision: Persistent connection with centralized edit queuing
decisions.alternatives_considered: REST-based polling for updates, HTTP/2 streaming with server push, and traditional WebSocket connections
decisions.trade_offs: REST polling introduces latency and overhead; HTTP/2 streaming requires complex implementation; WebSocket provides optimal real-time communication but needs proper connection management
decisions.rationale: WebSocket was chosen as the transport mechanism because it provides persistent, bidirectional communication that's essential for real-time collaborative editing. The centralized edit queuing approach ensures no data loss during brief network interruptions by buffering edits in a dedicated service with persistent storage rather than local memory. This design directly addresses the requirement to queue edits during brief network disconnections and reconcile changes when users reconnect.

decisions.alternatives_considered: Pure in-memory storage, pure persistent storage, and distributed database solutions
decisions.trade_offs: Pure in-memory storage offers best performance but no persistence; pure persistent storage provides durability but poor performance; distributed databases offer both but at high cost
decisions.rationale: This hybrid approach was selected to balance performance with cost constraints while meeting the 99.9% availability target. In-memory caching provides fast access to active documents while durable storage ensures data persistence and recovery capabilities. The system automatically flushes document snapshots to persistent storage every 5 seconds, providing a good balance between performance and durability within the $40,000 monthly budget.

security_controls.threat_model_summary: Primary threats include unauthorized document access via compromised user sessions, data integrity attacks where malicious users alter edit operations to cause convergence issues, network-based denial of service through connection flooding, and replay attacks during reconnection where stale edits are applied. Additionally, there's risk of edit queue manipulation by users attempting to gain unfair advantage in document convergence, and potential data loss if connection manager fails to properly queue edits during brief drops.
security_controls.authentication: OAuth2 with short-lived JWTs (30-minute expiry) issued by a dedicated Auth Service component, validated at the API gateway level using JWT middleware. Each WebSocket connection requires a valid token passed via query parameter or header during /connect endpoint handshake. Tokens include user_id and document_id claims for authorization checks. Per-operation token validation implemented within Document Engine to re-validate JWT claims (user_id, document_id) on each edit request before processing.
security_controls.authorization: Role-based access control using document ownership model where document creator has full permissions, collaborators have read/write access, and guests have read-only access. Authorization decisions made at Document Engine level by checking user permissions against document metadata stored in Document Storage. All edit operations validated against user's document access rights before processing. Per-user rate limiting implemented at Document Engine level for edit operations (e.g., 100 edits/sec) with circuit breaker logic to detect and temporarily block suspicious activity patterns. Implement cache invalidation strategy for document permissions with a short TTL (e.g., 5 seconds) and add a fallback mechanism that re-fetches document metadata from storage if cached data is not found or appears inconsistent during authorization checks.
security_controls.iam: User identities managed through OAuth2 provider (Auth0 or similar) with support for SSO and passwordless authentication. User sessions tracked via Connection Manager with automatic cleanup after 30 minutes of inactivity. Session tokens invalidated upon logout or after 24 hours of inactivity. No local user accounts maintained - all authentication handled externally.
security_controls.network_boundaries: API gateway acts as perimeter firewall with rate limiting (1000 req/sec per user) and IP-based restrictions for suspicious activity. Internal components communicate over encrypted gRPC/HTTP within VPC using mutual TLS authentication. Document Engine instances are isolated in separate subnets with security groups allowing only necessary inter-component traffic. Connection Manager and Edit Queue Service operate in dedicated subnet with restricted access to Document Storage. Strict VPC network segmentation implemented with security groups that limit inter-component communication to only necessary ports and protocols.
security_controls.secrets_and_encryption: All secrets (API keys, database credentials) stored in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation every 90 days. Data at rest encrypted using AWS KMS with customer-managed keys (CMKs). Data in transit encrypted using TLS 1.3 for all external communications and mutual TLS between internal services. JWT tokens signed with RSA-256 using rotating key pairs stored in Secrets Manager. Document content encrypted at rest using AES-256 with separate encryption keys per document, managed by a dedicated key management service (AWS KMS) rather than the Document Engine component directly. Each edit operation is cryptographically signed with HMAC-SHA256 before queuing to prevent tampering or replay attacks upon reconnection. Implement automated key rotation policy for per-document encryption keys (e.g., every 90 days) and establish a process to re-encrypt documents when keys are rotated. Additionally, log all key usage events for audit trails and implement key revocation procedures in case of suspected compromise.

reliability_design.scaling_strategy: The Document Engine is scaled using a sharded architecture with consistent hashing to distribute documents across multiple instances, eliminating single-writer bottlenecks. Scale horizontally using Kubernetes with auto-scaling based on concurrent edit operations. Connection Manager and Edit Queue Service scale independently with horizontal pods. Document Storage uses a hybrid approach (memory + disk) with periodic snapshot persistence, requiring minimal scaling. All components are deployed across multiple availability zones for high availability.
reliability_design.reliability: Document Engine implements sharded architecture with consistent hashing to prevent single points of failure at the document level. All document state changes processed through atomic operations. Connection Manager maintains persistent connections and handles disconnections gracefully by forwarding edits to centralized Edit Queue Service. Edit Queue Service stores queued edits in persistent storage (Redis) with 1-2 second flush intervals, using 10-second timeout for queues to prevent indefinite buffering. Document Storage uses write-through caching with automatic flushing every 5 seconds to disk for recovery purposes. All components use redundant deployments across availability zones with load balancing. Redis cluster with multi-master replication across availability zones implemented to prevent data loss during Redis instance failures.
reliability_design.disaster_recovery: Document Engine uses a sharded architecture with consistent hashing and atomic operations ensuring no data loss during brief disconnections. Edit Queue Service maintains queues in persistent storage (Redis) with 1-2 second flush intervals, using 10-second timeout to prevent indefinite buffering. Document Storage implements write-through caching with automatic flushing every 5 seconds to durable storage for recovery. All components are deployed across multiple availability zones with automatic failover mechanisms. No multi-region failover is implemented due to budget constraints and 99.9% availability target being achievable within single region. Implements cross-shard replication or a secondary routing mechanism that can redirect requests to alternative Document Engine instances if the primary shard becomes unavailable, ensuring no single shard failure impacts overall system availability.
reliability_design.observability: All components implement structured logging with correlation IDs, metrics collection (latency, throughput, error rates) via Prometheus, and distributed tracing using OpenTelemetry. Document Engine tracks edit processing time, queue depth, and conflict resolution metrics. Connection Manager monitors connection counts, heartbeat intervals, and reconnection success rates. Edit Queue Service logs queue operations, timeouts, and storage usage. Document Storage tracks read/write latency, snapshot frequency, and storage utilization. Alerting thresholds are set for 99.9% availability target with auto-remediation where possible. Added metric to track consecutive disconnection events per user with alerting threshold of 3+ disconnections within 5 minutes. Added specific metrics and alerts for conflict detection and resolution events in Document Engine, including frequency of conflicts, types of conflicts resolved, and time taken to resolve them.

Connection Manager loses WebSocket connection during brief network drop: Connection manager forwards edits to centralized Edit Queue Service which handles queuing with persistence, with 10-second timeout forcing reconciliation if user doesn't reconnect

Edit Queue Service memory overflow during high load: Sliding window algorithm limits queue size, automatic cleanup of completed/expired queues prevents memory exhaustion, persistent storage ensures no data loss
Document Storage disk failure during snapshot write: Write-through caching ensures data is flushed to durable storage every 5 seconds, with multiple availability zones providing redundancy

Network partition between Connection Manager and Document Engine: Load balancing handles failover, connection state maintained in persistent storage with automatic cleanup after 30 minutes of inactivity
User experiences 15-second network drop during editing: Centralized edit queue buffers operations for up to 10 seconds before forcing reconciliation, ensuring no data loss

Multiple users edit same document simultaneously with conflicting changes: Operational Transformation handles conflict resolution at the Document Engine level, ensuring convergence to same final state regardless of order
Document Engine memory leak during high concurrent usage: Kubernetes auto-scaling and memory monitoring detect and restart unhealthy pods automatically

Edit Queue Service becomes unavailable during reconnection: Retry mechanism with exponential backoff in Connection Manager when forwarding edits to Edit Queue Service, and local buffering capability on the client-side to temporarily store edits if the queue service is unreachable

findings.issue: JWT tokens are validated at API gateway level but not re-validated at the Document Engine level for each edit operation, creating a potential window for token misuse if a token is stolen and not immediately revoked.
findings.recommendation: Implement per-operation JWT validation within the Document Engine to re-check token claims (user_id, document_id) on every edit request before processing. This prevents scenarios where a compromised token could be used to make unauthorized edits after initial connection.

findings.issue: Rate limiting is implemented at Document Engine level but only for edit operations; there's no rate limiting on WebSocket connection attempts or reconnection requests, which could allow DoS attacks through excessive connection churn.
findings.recommendation: Add rate limiting on /connect endpoint and /reconnect messages to prevent abuse from repeated connection attempts. Consider implementing a sliding window algorithm with limits such as 10 connections/second per IP/user.

findings.issue: Edit operations are cryptographically signed with HMAC-SHA256 before queuing, but the signature verification is only performed upon reconnection. If a malicious user tampers with queued edits, they could potentially cause conflicts or data corruption during reconciliation.
findings.recommendation: Perform signature validation immediately upon receiving an edit in the Edit Queue Service, not just at reconnection time. This prevents tampering of queued edits and ensures that only legitimate edits from authenticated users are stored.

findings.issue: While internal services communicate over encrypted channels using mutual TLS, there's no explicit mention of network segmentation or firewall rules restricting inter-component communication beyond basic port/protocol restrictions.
findings.recommendation: Implement strict security group rules that limit inter-component traffic to only necessary ports and protocols. Add network ACLs for additional filtering between subnets, especially between the Connection Manager and Edit Queue Service where sensitive edit data flows.

findings.issue: Per-document encryption keys are managed by AWS KMS but there's no clear process defined for handling key revocation or re-encryption of documents when keys are rotated, which could lead to data accessibility issues during key rotation events.
findings.recommendation: Define a clear document re-encryption workflow that triggers upon key rotation. Implement a background job that periodically checks for rotated keys and re-encrypts affected documents with new keys, ensuring no service interruption or data loss.

findings.issue: High Redis usage for 100K queued operations with 10-second timeouts could exceed budget if concurrent users increase beyond current estimate. The service is the most expensive component at ~$20,000/month for Redis alone, assuming 500,000 documents with 50 concurrent editors (25M total connections) and 100K queued operations.
findings.recommendation: Monitor actual queue depths and implement dynamic scaling of Redis instances to prevent over-provisioning. Consider implementing a more aggressive cleanup policy for expired queues if they're not being cleared quickly enough.

findings.issue: The Document Engine is designed with sharding but assumes 50 editors per document. If this limit is exceeded, additional horizontal scaling will be required which could push costs over budget without explicit headroom for traffic spikes.
findings.recommendation: Implement explicit monitoring and alerting on concurrent editor limits to proactively scale before hitting hard constraints.

findings.issue: Supporting 20,000 WebSocket connections with backpressure handling requires significant compute resources. The architecture assumes these are handled efficiently but doesn't account for bursty traffic patterns or connection churn that could increase costs.
findings.recommendation: Add metrics tracking on connection churn and implement adaptive connection pooling strategies to optimize resource usage during peak times.

findings.issue: The Edit Queue Service uses Redis with multi-master replication across availability zones, but there's no explicit mention of Redis cluster failover handling or automatic promotion of replicas during master failure. Additionally, the centralized edit queuing approach creates a potential bottleneck if Redis becomes unavailable.
findings.recommendation: Implement Redis Sentinel or use managed Redis service with automatic failover capabilities to ensure seamless transition during master node failures. Add explicit monitoring and alerting for Redis cluster health, including metrics for replica synchronization status and failover events. Consider implementing a secondary queuing mechanism (e.g., temporary local buffering) as a fallback when Redis is unreachable to prevent complete system degradation during brief Redis outages.

findings.issue: The system targets 99.9% availability but relies on a sharded Document Engine architecture that assumes consistent hashing will distribute load evenly. If certain documents become hotspots, the system may not maintain the required availability SLA due to resource contention or single shard failures.
findings.recommendation: Implement dynamic sharding with load balancing metrics and auto-scaling triggers based on document-level performance indicators. Add circuit breaker patterns at Document Engine level to isolate failing shards and prevent cascading failures that could impact overall availability. Monitor and alert on shard utilization ratios to proactively address hotspots before they affect SLA compliance.

findings.issue: The document storage flush interval is 5 seconds, which may not meet RPO requirements for brief network interruptions if the system needs to guarantee no data loss within sub-second timeframes. Additionally, while snapshots are taken periodically, there's no explicit mention of how quickly these can be restored during recovery scenarios.
findings.recommendation: Reduce document storage flush interval to 1-2 seconds to better align with RPO requirements for brief interruptions. Implement incremental snapshotting and faster recovery procedures that can restore document state within 30 seconds from the last flush point. Add automated rollback testing to verify recovery times meet SLA requirements.

findings.issue: While comprehensive logging and metrics are implemented, there's no mention of specific monitoring for conflict resolution performance or frequency. The system may not adequately detect when conflicts are occurring too frequently or taking too long to resolve, which could impact user experience and system reliability.
findings.recommendation: Add dedicated metrics for conflict resolution latency, frequency of conflicts per document, and time taken to converge edits from multiple users. Implement alerting thresholds that trigger when conflict resolution times exceed 500ms or when conflict frequency increases by more than 200% over a 10-minute window. Add correlation IDs across all components to trace edit operations from client through queue to final document state.

findings.issue: The failure scenario analysis mentions that Connection Manager forwards edits to Edit Queue Service during reconnection, but doesn't specify how the system handles cases where both Connection Manager and Edit Queue Service become unavailable simultaneously. There's also no mention of how client-side local buffering is handled if the queue service is unreachable.
findings.recommendation: Implement a multi-layered queuing strategy where client-side local buffering is used as primary fallback when connection manager cannot reach edit queue service, with automatic retry mechanisms and exponential backoff. Add circuit breaker patterns at Connection Manager level to detect and isolate Edit Queue Service unavailability, preventing cascading failures. Implement health checks that monitor both components' availability and automatically redirect traffic when one component becomes unavailable.

findings.issue: The architecture assumes a WebSocket-based persistent connection for all real-time operations, but this approach creates severe scaling bottlenecks at the stated volume. With 500,000 documents and up to 50 concurrent editors per document, you're looking at 25 million simultaneous WebSocket connections. The Connection Manager component is designed to handle 20,000 concurrent WebSocket connections, which would require 1,250 instances just to support the peak load - a massive overengineering that will exceed the $40K budget and create operational complexity.
findings.recommendation: Replace persistent WebSocket connections with a hybrid approach: use long-lived WebSockets for active sessions but implement HTTP/2 streaming with server push for low-activity documents. This would reduce connection overhead by 95% while maintaining real-time update semantics. Additionally, implement a connection pooling strategy where users are grouped into connection pools of 10-20 concurrent editors, reducing total connection count to ~250,000 connections (still within reasonable limits). The current approach will create an unmanageable number of connections that will overwhelm both your infrastructure and the Connection Manager's capacity to scale.

findings.issue: The architecture has two separate components claiming responsibility for edit queuing: the Connection Manager forwards edits to the Edit Queue Service upon reconnection, but the system also maintains local client-side buffering capabilities. This duplication creates a fundamental architectural flaw where the same edit operation could be queued twice - once in the centralized service and once locally. The system lacks a clear single source of truth for edit queuing, leading to potential data inconsistencies and race conditions during reconciliation.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate local client-side buffering entirely and implement a strict centralized queuing model. Remove the client-side buffering capability from Connection Manager and ensure all edits are queued only in the Edit Queue Service. This eliminates the duplication of responsibility, reduces complexity, and prevents potential race conditions where the same edit might be applied twice during reconciliation. The system should rely solely on the Edit Queue Service for all queuing operations with proper cryptographic signatures to prevent tampering.

findings.issue: The Document Engine uses consistent hashing for sharding, but this approach couples the sharding logic directly to the Document Engine's architecture. The system assumes that each document will be permanently assigned to a specific shard, which creates a single point of failure risk and prevents efficient rebalancing when scaling. This coupling also makes it impossible to implement dynamic load balancing or handle hotspots where certain documents receive disproportionately high edit loads.
findings.recommendation: Implement a dynamic sharding strategy with a separate routing layer that can redistribute documents based on current load conditions. Remove the direct dependency of Document Engine instances on consistent hashing and instead use a centralized routing service that maintains shard assignments dynamically. This allows for better load distribution, eliminates single points of failure, and enables more efficient scaling when certain documents become hotspots. The routing layer should also maintain metadata about document access patterns to optimize sharding decisions.

findings.issue: The Document Engine claims to handle up to 10,000 concurrent edit operations per second with <5ms average latency, but the hybrid OT/CRDT approach creates a severe performance bottleneck. Operational Transformation requires complex state tracking and transformation calculations that scale poorly with concurrent edits, while CRDTs introduce significant computational overhead for structural changes. At peak load (50 editors × 250,000 documents = 12.5 million concurrent edit operations), this system will likely exceed its performance targets by orders of magnitude.
findings.recommendation: Implement a tiered conflict resolution approach where simple text operations use OT for performance, while complex structural changes are batched and processed asynchronously. Introduce a separate conflict resolution queue that can handle bursts of complex operations without impacting real-time edit processing. Additionally, consider using a more efficient CRDT implementation like LWW-Element-Set or G-Counter for specific use cases rather than applying CRDTs universally. The system should also implement pre-processing to identify and batch similar operations to reduce the complexity of conflict resolution.

findings.area: Data Loss Risk Through Multiple Components
findings.issue: The architecture has multiple points where data loss could occur: Document Engine flushes snapshots every 5 seconds, but this is insufficient for a system that must handle brief network drops. The Edit Queue Service uses Redis with 1-2 second flush intervals, but there's no mechanism to ensure all edits are durably stored before acknowledgment. Additionally, the Connection Manager forwards edits to the Edit Queue Service without local buffering, creating potential data loss if the queue service is temporarily unavailable.
findings.recommendation: Implement a write-ahead logging (WAL) approach across all components with mandatory durability guarantees for edit operations. All edits must be written to a durable log before being acknowledged to clients, and the system should maintain a separate recovery queue that ensures no edit is lost during brief network interruptions. The current design lacks any mechanism to guarantee that edits are durably stored before acknowledgment, which violates the requirement to prevent data loss during brief network interruptions.

findings.issue: The architecture has multiple overlapping security controls that create operational complexity and potential gaps. For example, both Document Engine and Connection Manager perform JWT validation, but they may not be synchronized in their validation logic. Additionally, the cryptographic signatures for edits are implemented at the Edit Queue Service level, but there's no mechanism to validate these signatures when edits are forwarded from Connection Manager to Edit Queue Service, creating a potential attack vector.
findings.recommendation: Consolidate all JWT validation into a single service (API Gateway or Auth Service) and remove redundant validations. Implement a unified signature verification process that occurs at the point of edit submission rather than relying on separate signature generation and verification steps. Ensure that all security controls operate in a consistent manner across components to avoid gaps in protection.

architecture_stages.characteristics: A minimal viable product that focuses on core collaborative editing functionality with simplified infrastructure and reduced feature set. The system maintains real-time editing capabilities but removes complex conflict resolution mechanisms, reduces scalability assumptions, and simplifies the architecture to validate the concept quickly.
architecture_stages.purpose: Validate core collaborative editing concept with minimal investment while proving the fundamental value proposition of real-time document collaboration

blueprint.product: A collaborative document editor that allows multiple users to simultaneously edit the same document and see each other's changes in real-time. The system must handle network interruptions gracefully by queuing edits during brief disconnections and reconciling changes when users reconnect, ensuring all users eventually see the same final document version regardless of editing order or timing.

components.name: Document Engine
components.description: Core component responsible for managing document state, applying edits, and handling conflict resolution using Operational Transformation (OT) or Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDT). Processes real-time edits from users and maintains a consistent document view across all clients. Handles the convergence of edits from multiple concurrent editors into a single final document state regardless of order or timing. Scales horizontally to support 500,000 documents with up to 50 concurrent editors per document, operating within the $40,000 monthly budget constraint. Maintains 99.9% availability target through replication and failover mechanisms. Uses a hybrid approach of OT for simple edits and CRDT for complex structural changes to optimize performance while ensuring consistency. Stores document state in memory with periodic snapshots to disk for recovery purposes. Processes up to 10,000 concurrent edit operations per second across all documents, with each operation taking less than 5ms on average. Implements a sharded architecture where documents are distributed across multiple instances based on consistent hashing to enable true horizontal scaling. The component is the only one that can modify document state directly, ensuring consistency through atomic operations. Uses a persistent connection model for real-time updates and handles network disconnections by queuing edits in a centralized service before reconciliation upon reconnection. Maintains a 10-second timeout for edit queues to prevent indefinite buffering of stale changes. Processes edit history in batches of 100 operations to optimize memory usage and reduce latency during conflict resolution. Implements a two-phase commit protocol for critical document modifications to ensure atomicity across distributed systems. This component is the only one that can modify document state directly, ensuring consistency through atomic operations. Decomposed into separate services for document state management, conflict resolution algorithms, and atomic write operations to improve scalability and maintainability.

components.name: Connection Manager
components.description: Manages real-time WebSocket connections between clients and Document Engine components. Handles connection lifecycle events including establishment, disconnection, and reconnection. Forwards edits to the centralized Edit Queue Service upon reconnection instead of queuing locally. Implements a backpressure mechanism to prevent overwhelming the system during high-traffic periods. Maintains connection state for up to 50 concurrent editors per document with automatic cleanup of inactive connections after 30 minutes of inactivity. Uses a connection pooling strategy to optimize resource utilization and reduce latency during connection establishment. Tracks user presence and session information for each document. Implements a heartbeat mechanism to detect and handle dead connections proactively. Handles client-side reconnection logic including resynchronization of local edit queue with server state. Processes up to 20,000 concurrent WebSocket connections across all documents while maintaining <10ms latency for connection establishment. Operates within the $40,000 monthly budget constraint and maintains 99.9% availability target through redundant connection handling. Uses a distributed architecture with multiple instances to ensure no single point of failure. Implements automatic load balancing between Document Engine instances based on current connection count and resource utilization. Implements retry mechanism with exponential backoff when forwarding edits to Edit Queue Service, and adds local buffering capability on the client-side to temporarily store edits if the queue service is unreachable.

components.name: Edit Queue Service
components.description: Dedicated service for storing and managing edit queues during network disconnections. Maintains a queue per user per document with automatic cleanup of completed or expired queues. Stores queued edits in persistent storage (Redis with persistence) to prevent data loss during system failures. Implements a priority-based queuing system where newer edits take precedence over older ones to minimize staleness. Uses a time-based expiration mechanism to prevent indefinite buffering of edits, with a default timeout of 10 seconds before forcing reconciliation. Processes up to 100,000 queued edit operations across all documents while maintaining <5ms latency for queue operations. Handles concurrent access to queues using atomic operations to ensure data integrity during simultaneous read/write operations. Implements a sliding window algorithm to limit queue size and prevent memory exhaustion. The service is optimized for high-throughput scenarios with minimal latency impact on real-time editing performance. Operates within the $40,000 monthly budget constraint and maintains 99.9% availability target through replication and failover mechanisms. Uses a distributed architecture with multiple instances to ensure no single point of failure. Implements automatic scaling based on queue depth and system load to optimize resource utilization. Adds cryptographic signatures (e.g., HMAC-SHA256) to all messages forwarded from Connection Manager to Edit Queue Service, ensuring that the edit queue contents cannot be modified in transit and that only legitimate connection managers can submit edits for queuing.

components.name: Document Storage
components.description: Persistent storage layer for document snapshots, edit history, and metadata. Uses a combination of in-memory cache for active documents and durable storage for archived content. Implements a write-through caching strategy with automatic flushing to persistent storage every 5 seconds for active documents. Maintains document version history with support for rollback operations and audit trails. Handles large document sizes up to 10MB per document with optimized storage formats for efficient retrieval and processing. Uses a distributed storage system with replication across multiple availability zones to ensure high availability and durability. Implements automatic backup and recovery procedures with point-in-time restore capabilities. Processes up to 50,000 document read/write operations per second while maintaining <10ms latency for critical operations. Operates within the $40,000 monthly budget constraint and maintains 99.9% availability target through replication and failover mechanisms. Uses a hybrid storage approach combining SSDs for active documents with cheaper storage for archived content. Implements automatic compaction of edit history to reduce storage overhead while maintaining version integrity. The component ensures no data loss during brief network interruptions by persisting document state regularly and providing recovery mechanisms for disconnected sessions. Implements write-ahead logging (WAL) or similar transactional persistence mechanism on top of the 5-second flush interval to ensure that all edit operations are durably recorded before being acknowledged to clients, meeting RPO requirements for brief interruptions.

security_controls.threat_model_summary: Primary threats include unauthorized document access via compromised user sessions, data integrity attacks where malicious users alter edit operations to cause convergence issues, network-based denial of service through connection flooding, and replay attacks during reconnection where stale edits are applied. Additionally, there's risk of edit queue manipulation by users attempting to gain unfair advantage in document convergence, and potential data loss if connection manager fails to properly queue edits during brief drops.
security_controls.authentication: OAuth2 with short-lived JWTs (30-minute expiry) issued by a dedicated Auth Service component, validated at the API gateway level using JWT middleware. Each WebSocket connection requires a valid token passed via query parameter or header during /connect endpoint handshake. Tokens include user_id and document_id claims for authorization checks. Per-operation token validation implemented within Document Engine to re-validate JWT claims (user_id, document_id) on each edit request before processing.
security_controls.authorization: Role-based access control using document ownership model where document creator has full permissions, collaborators have read/write access, and guests have read-only access. Authorization decisions made at Document Engine level by checking user permissions against document metadata stored in Document Storage. All edit operations validated against user's document access rights before processing. Per-user rate limiting implemented at Document Engine level for edit operations (e.g., 100 edits/sec) with circuit breaker logic to detect and temporarily block suspicious activity patterns. Implement cache invalidation strategy for document permissions with a short TTL (e.g., 5 seconds) and add a fallback mechanism that re-fetches document metadata from storage if cached data is not found or appears inconsistent during authorization checks.
security_controls.iam: User identities managed through OAuth2 provider (Auth0 or similar) with support for SSO and passwordless authentication. User sessions tracked via Connection Manager with automatic cleanup after 30 minutes of inactivity. Session tokens invalidated upon logout or after 24 hours of inactivity. No local user accounts maintained - all authentication handled externally.
security_controls.network_boundaries: API gateway acts as perimeter firewall with rate limiting (1000 req/sec per user) and IP-based restrictions for suspicious activity. Internal components communicate over encrypted gRPC/HTTP within VPC using mutual TLS authentication. Document Engine instances are isolated in separate subnets with security groups allowing only necessary inter-component traffic. Connection Manager and Edit Queue Service operate in dedicated subnet with restricted access to Document Storage. Strict VPC network segmentation implemented with security groups that limit inter-component communication to only necessary ports and protocols.
security_controls.secrets_and_encryption: All secrets (API keys, database credentials) stored in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation every 90 days. Data at rest encrypted using AWS KMS with customer-managed keys (CMKs). Data in transit encrypted using TLS 1.3 for all external communications and mutual TLS between internal services. JWT tokens signed with RSA-256 using rotating key pairs stored in Secrets Manager. Document content encrypted at rest using AES-256 with separate encryption keys per document, managed by a dedicated key management service (AWS KMS) rather than the Document Engine component directly. Each edit operation is cryptographically signed with HMAC-SHA256 before queuing to prevent tampering or replay attacks upon reconnection. Implement automated key rotation policy for per-document encryption keys (e.g., every 90 days) and establish a process to re-encrypt documents when keys are rotated. Additionally, log all key usage events for audit trails and implement key revocation procedures in case of suspected compromise.

threats.issue: JWT tokens are validated at API gateway level but not re-validated at the Document Engine level for each edit operation, creating a potential window for token misuse if a token is stolen and not immediately revoked.
threats.recommendation: Implement per-operation JWT validation within the Document Engine to re-check token claims (user_id, document_id) on every edit request before processing. This prevents scenarios where a compromised token could be used to make unauthorized edits after initial connection.

threats.issue: Rate limiting is implemented at Document Engine level but only for edit operations; there's no rate limiting on WebSocket connection attempts or reconnection requests, which could allow DoS attacks through excessive connection churn.
threats.recommendation: Add rate limiting on /connect endpoint and /reconnect messages to prevent abuse from repeated connection attempts. Consider implementing a sliding window algorithm with limits such as 10 connections/second per IP/user.

threats.issue: Edit operations are cryptographically signed with HMAC-SHA256 before queuing, but the signature verification is only performed upon reconnection. If a malicious user tampers with queued edits, they could potentially cause conflicts or data corruption during reconciliation.
threats.recommendation: Perform signature validation immediately upon receiving an edit in the Edit Queue Service, not just at reconnection time. This prevents tampering of queued edits and ensures that only legitimate edits from authenticated users are stored.

threats.issue: While internal services communicate over encrypted channels using mutual TLS, there's no explicit mention of network segmentation or firewall rules restricting inter-component communication beyond basic port/protocol restrictions.
threats.recommendation: Implement strict security group rules that limit inter-component traffic to only necessary ports and protocols. Add network ACLs for additional filtering between subnets, especially between the Connection Manager and Edit Queue Service where sensitive edit data flows.

threats.issue: Per-document encryption keys are managed by AWS KMS but there's no clear process defined for handling key revocation or re-encryption of documents when keys are rotated, which could lead to data accessibility issues during key rotation events.
threats.recommendation: Define a clear document re-encryption workflow that triggers upon key rotation. Implement a background job that periodically checks for rotated keys and re-encrypts affected documents with new keys, ensuring no service interruption or data loss.

blueprint.infrastructure: The system uses a distributed architecture with multiple components deployed across cloud infrastructure. The Document Engine and Connection Manager are horizontally scalable services that can be scaled independently based on load requirements. The Edit Queue Service operates as a dedicated microservice with optimized persistent storage for high-throughput scenarios. Document Storage utilizes a hybrid storage approach combining in-memory caching with durable persistent storage for active documents. All components are deployed with redundancy across multiple availability zones to ensure 99.9% availability target. Network traffic is load balanced using a combination of DNS-based routing and application-level load balancing. The system uses containerization with orchestration via Kubernetes for deployment management and scaling automation. Infrastructure monitoring and alerting systems are implemented to track performance metrics and ensure service level agreements are maintained within the $40,000 monthly budget constraint. Redis cluster with multi-master replication across availability zones is implemented to prevent data loss during Redis instance failures, ensuring 99.9% availability target compliance for Edit Queue Service.
blueprint.scaling_strategy: The Document Engine is scaled using a sharded architecture with consistent hashing to distribute documents across multiple instances, eliminating single-writer bottlenecks. Scale horizontally using Kubernetes with auto-scaling based on concurrent edit operations. Connection Manager and Edit Queue Service scale independently with horizontal pods. Document Storage uses a hybrid approach (memory + disk) with periodic snapshot persistence, requiring minimal scaling. All components are deployed across multiple availability zones for high availability.
blueprint.reliability: Document Engine implements sharded architecture with consistent hashing to prevent single points of failure at the document level. All document state changes processed through atomic operations. Connection Manager maintains persistent connections and handles disconnections gracefully by forwarding edits to centralized Edit Queue Service. Edit Queue Service stores queued edits in persistent storage (Redis) with 1-2 second flush intervals, using 10-second timeout for queues to prevent indefinite buffering. Document Storage uses write-through caching with automatic flushing every 5 seconds to disk for recovery purposes. All components use redundant deployments across availability zones with load balancing. Redis cluster with multi-master replication across availability zones implemented to prevent data loss during Redis instance failures.
blueprint.disaster_recovery: Document Engine uses a sharded architecture with consistent hashing and atomic operations ensuring no data loss during brief disconnections. Edit Queue Service maintains queues in persistent storage (Redis) with 1-2 second flush intervals, using 10-second timeout to prevent indefinite buffering. Document Storage implements write-through caching with automatic flushing every 5 seconds to durable storage for recovery. All components are deployed across multiple availability zones with automatic failover mechanisms. No multi-region failover is implemented due to budget constraints and 99.9% availability target being achievable within single region. Implements cross-shard replication or a secondary routing mechanism that can redirect requests to alternative Document Engine instances if the primary shard becomes unavailable, ensuring no single shard failure impacts overall system availability.
blueprint.observability: All components implement structured logging with correlation IDs, metrics collection (latency, throughput, error rates) via Prometheus, and distributed tracing using OpenTelemetry. Document Engine tracks edit processing time, queue depth, and conflict resolution metrics. Connection Manager monitors connection counts, heartbeat intervals, and reconnection success rates. Edit Queue Service logs queue operations, timeouts, and storage usage. Document Storage tracks read/write latency, snapshot frequency, and storage utilization. Alerting thresholds are set for 99.9% availability target with auto-remediation where possible. Added metric to track consecutive disconnection events per user with alerting threshold of 3+ disconnections within 5 minutes. Added specific metrics and alerts for conflict detection and resolution events in Document Engine, including frequency of conflicts, types of conflicts resolved, and time taken to resolve them.

decisions.rationale: This approach was chosen because it provides the best balance of consistency guarantees and performance for collaborative editing. OT ensures strong consistency for simple text operations while CRDT handles complex structural changes where OT might be insufficient. The hybrid approach allows for optimal performance while maintaining data integrity under all conditions, meeting the requirement to prevent data loss during brief network interruptions. A unified conflict resolution pipeline was implemented to handle transitions between OT and CRDT operations consistently.

decisions.alternatives_considered: Multi-writer with optimistic locking, single-writer with sharding, and distributed consensus protocols like Raft or Paxos
decisions.trade_offs: Single-writer provides strong consistency but limits parallelism; multi-writer offers better throughput but introduces complexity in conflict resolution; distributed consensus protocols provide strong guarantees but require significant overhead
decisions.rationale: This decision was made to ensure data consistency and prevent race conditions during edit application while maintaining reasonable performance. The sharded architecture with consistent hashing allows for true horizontal scaling across multiple Document Engine instances, eliminating the single-writer bottleneck that would otherwise create a severe scalability constraint. This design choice directly addresses the requirement that all users see identical final document versions regardless of edit order or timing, while keeping complexity manageable within the budget constraints.

The centralized edit queuing approach ensures no data loss during brief network interruptions by buffering edits in a dedicated service with persistent storage rather than local memory.
